a1.he: תַּלְמוּד לוֹמַר: ״פֶּטֶר חֲמוֹר״ ״פֶּטֶר חֲמוֹר״ שְׁנֵי פְּעָמִים — פִּטְרֵי חֲמוֹרִים אָמַרְתִּי לְךָ, וְלֹא פִּטְרֵי סוּסִים וּגְמַלִּים.

a2.he: פָּרֵיךְ רַב אַחַאי: אִי כְּתַב רַחֲמָנָא חַד, הֲוָה אָמֵינָא דָּבָר שֶׁהָיָה בַּכְּלָל, וְיָצָא מִן הַכְּלָל לְלַמֵּד, לֹא לְלַמֵּד עַל עַצְמוֹ יָצָא אֶלָּא לְלַמֵּד עַל הַכְּלָל כּוּלּוֹ יָצָא, וּלְעוֹלָם בְּשֶׂה.

a3.he: כְּתַב רַחֲמָנָא ״פֶּטֶר חֲמוֹר״ אַחֲרִינָא, פִּטְרֵי חֲמוֹרִים וְלֹא פִּטְרֵי סוּסִים וּגְמַלִּים, וְאֵימָא: מַעֲטִינְהוּ מִשֶׂה, וּלְעוֹלָם בְּכׇל דָּבָר!

a4.he: אִם כֵּן, לִכְתּוֹב רַחֲמָנָא: ״פֶּטֶר חֲמוֹר תִּפְדֶּה בְשֶׂה״ וַ״חֲמוֹר תִּפְדֶּה בְשֶׂה״. ״פֶּטֶר חֲמוֹר תִּפְדֶּה בְשֶׂה״, ״פֶּטֶר חֲמוֹר תִּפְדֶּה בְשֶׂה״ לְמָה לִי? פִּטְרֵי חֲמוֹרִים אָמַרְתִּי לְךָ, וְלֹא פִּטְרֵי סוּסִים וּגְמַלִּים.

a5.he: וְתַנָּא דִידַן, לְמַעוֹטֵי סוּסִים וּגְמַלִּים, מְנָא לֵיהּ?

a6.he: אָמַר רַב פָּפָּא: כׇּל מִקְנְךָ תִּזָּכָר — כָּלַל, שׁוֹר וָשֶׂה וַחֲמוֹר — פָּרַט, כְּלָל וּפְרָט — אֵין בַּכְּלָל אֶלָּא מַה שֶּׁבַּפְּרָט, שׁוֹר וָשֶׂה וַחֲמוֹר — אִין, מִידֵּי אַחֲרִינָא — לָא.

a7.he: וְרַבִּי יוֹסֵי הַגְּלִילִי? ״פֶּטֶר״ הִפְסִיק הָעִנְיָן, וְרַבָּנַן? וָי״ו הֲדַר עָרְבֵיהּ קְרָא.

a8.he: וְרַבִּי יוֹסֵי הַגְּלִילִי? לָא לִכְתּוֹב לָא וָי״ו וְלָא ״פֶּטֶר״.

a9.he: וְרַבָּנַן? אַיְּידֵי דְּהָא קְדוּשַּׁת דָּמִים, וְהָא קְדוּשַּׁת הַגּוּף — פָּסֵיק לְהוּ וַהֲדַר עָרֵיב לְהוּ.

a10.he: אִיבַּעְיָא לְהוּ: פָּרָה שֶׁיָּלְדָה מִין חֲמוֹר, וְיֵשׁ בּוֹ מִקְצָת סִימָנִין — מַהוּ?

a11.he: עֵז שֶׁיָּלְדָה מִין רָחֵל, וְרָחֵל שֶׁיָּלְדָה מִין עֵז, דְּכִי יֵשׁ מִקְצָת סִימָנִין — חַיֶּיבֶת בִּבְכוֹרָה, דְּהָא טְהוֹרָה וְהָא טְהוֹרָה, הָא קְדוּשַּׁת הַגּוּף וְהָא קְדוּשַּׁת הַגּוּף.

a12.he: הָכָא, דְּהָא טְמֵאָה וְהָא טְהוֹרָה, הָא קְדוּשַּׁת הַגּוּף וְהָא קְדוּשַּׁת דָּמִים — לָא, אוֹ דִלְמָא: כֵּיוָן דְּאִידֵּי וְאִידֵּי בְּנֵי מִיקְדָּשׁ בִּבְכוֹרָה — קָדוֹשׁ?

a13.he: וְאִם תִּמְצֵי לוֹמַר: כֵּיוָן דְּאִידֵּי וְאִידֵּי מִיקְדָּשׁ בִּבְכוֹרָה קָדוֹשׁ, חֲמוֹר שֶׁיָּלְדָה מִין סוּס מַהוּ? הָכָא וַדַּאי לָא בַּת מִיקְדָּשׁ בִּבְכוֹרָה הוּא, אוֹ דִלְמָא כֵּיוָן דְּמִין טְמֵאָה הוּא קָדוֹשׁ?

a14.he: אִם תִּמְצָא לוֹמַר: כֵּיוָן דְּמִין טְמֵאָה הוּא קָדוֹשׁ, פָּרָה שֶׁיָּלְדָה מִין סוּס מַהוּ? הָכָא וַדַּאי הָא טְהוֹרָה וְהָא טְמֵאָה, הָא בַּת מִיקְדָּשׁ בִּבְכוֹרָה וְהָא לָא בַּת מִיקְדָּשׁ בִּבְכוֹרָה, אוֹ דִלְמָא סִימָנִין מִילְּתָא הִיא?

a15.he: תָּא שְׁמַע: בְּהֵמָה טְהוֹרָה שֶׁיָּלְדָה מִין בְּהֵמָה טְמֵאָה — פְּטוּרָה מִן הַבְּכוֹרָה, אִם יֵשׁ בּוֹ מִקְצָת סִימָנִין — חַיֶּיבֶת בִּבְכוֹרָה. מַאי לָאו אֲפִילּוּ פָּרָה שֶׁיָּלְדָה מִין סוּס? לֹא, פָּרָה שֶׁיָּלְדָה מִין חֲמוֹר.

a16.he: תָּא שְׁמַע: פָּרָה שֶׁיָּלְדָה מִין חֲמוֹר, וַחֲמוֹר שֶׁיָּלְדָה מִין סוּס — פְּטוּרָה מִן הַבְּכוֹרָה, אִם יֵשׁ בּוֹ מִקְצָת סִימָנִין — חַיֶּיבֶת בִּבְכוֹרָה. מַאי לָאו אַתַּרְוַיְיהוּ? לָא, אַפָּרָה שֶׁיָּלְדָה מִין חֲמוֹר.

a17.he: אֲבָל חֲמוֹר שֶׁיָּלְדָה מִין סוּס, לְמַאי קָתָנֵי לַהּ? לִפְטוּרָא? פְּשִׁיטָא! הַשְׁתָּא, וּמָה פָּרָה שֶׁיָּלְדָה מִין חֲמוֹר, דְּאִידֵּי וְאִידֵּי בְּנֵי מִיקְדָּשׁ בִּבְכוֹרָה נִינְהוּ, אָמְרַתְּ: אִם יֵשׁ בּוֹ מִקְצָת סִימָנִין — אִין, וְאִי לָא — לָא, חֲמוֹר שֶׁיָּלְדָה מִין סוּס מִיבַּעְיָא?

a18.he: אִיצְטְרִיךְ, סָלְקָא דַּעְתָּךְ: הָתָם הוּא דְּיֵשׁ לָהּ קַרְנַיִם, וְהָא אֵין לָהּ קַרְנַיִם; הָא פַּרְסוֹתֶיהָ סְדוּקוֹת, וְהָא פַּרְסוֹתֶיהָ קְלוּטוֹת.

a19.he: אֲבָל הָכָא, דְּאִידֵּי וְאִידֵּי אֵין לָהּ קַרְנַיִם, אִידֵּי וְאִידֵּי פַּרְסוֹתֶיהָ קְלוּטוֹת, אֵימָא חֲמוֹר אָדוֹם בְּעָלְמָא הוּא, קָמַשְׁמַע לַן.

a20.he: וּמָה הֵן בַּאֲכִילָה כּוּ׳. לְמָה לִי לְמִיתְנֵי ״שֶׁהַיּוֹצֵא״?

a21.he: סִימָנָא בְּעָלְמָא הוּא, דְּלָא תִּיחַלַּף לָךְ, דְּלָא תֵּימָא: זִיל בָּתְרֵיהּ דִּידֵיהּ, וְהַאי טָהוֹר מְעַלְּיָא הוּא, וְהַאי טָמֵא מְעַלְּיָא הוּא, אֶלָּא זִיל בָּתַר אִימֵּיהּ.

a22.he: מְנָא הָנֵי מִילֵּי? דְּתָנוּ רַבָּנַן: ״אַךְ אֶת זֶה לֹא תֹאכְלוּ מִמַּעֲלֵי הַגֵּרָה וּמִמַּפְרִיסֵי הַפַּרְסָה״ — יֵשׁ לְךָ שֶׁהוּא מַעֲלֵה גֵרָה וּמַפְרִיס פַּרְסָה וְאִי אַתָּה אוֹכְלוֹ, וְאֵיזֶה זֶה? טָהוֹר שֶׁנּוֹלַד מִן הַטָּמֵא. אוֹ אֵינוֹ אֶלָּא טָמֵא הַנּוֹלָד מִן הַטָּהוֹר, וּמַאי ״מִמַּעֲלֵי הַגֵּרָה וּמִמַּפְרִיסֵי הַפַּרְסָה״?

b1.he: הָכִי קָאָמַר: דָּבָר הַבָּא מִמַּעֲלֵי הַגֵּרָה וּמִמַּפְרִיסֵי הַפַּרְסָה לָא תֵּיכוּל, תַּלְמוּד לוֹמַר: ״גָּמָל... טָמֵא הוּא״ — הוּא טָמֵא, וְאֵין טָמֵא הַנּוֹלָד מִן הַטָּהוֹר טָמֵא אֶלָּא טָהוֹר.

b2.he: רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן אוֹמֵר: ״גָּמָל״ ״גָּמָל״ שְׁנֵי פְּעָמִים, אֶחָד גָּמָל הַנּוֹלָד מִן הַגְּמַלָּה, וְאֶחָד גָּמָל הַנּוֹלָד מִן הַפָּרָה.

b3.he: וְרַבָּנַן, הַאי ״גָּמָל״ ״גָּמָל״ מַאי עָבְדִי לֵיהּ? חַד לֶאֱסוֹר עַצְמוֹ, וְחַד לֶאֱסוֹר חֲלָבוֹ. וְרַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן, לֶאֱסוֹר חֲלָבוֹ מְנָא לֵיהּ? נָפְקָא לֵיהּ מֵ״אֶת הַגָּמָל״. וְרַבָּנַן, ״אֶתִּים״ לָא דָּרְשִׁי.

b4.he: כִּדְתַנְיָא: שִׁמְעוֹן הָעַמְסוֹנִי הָיָה דּוֹרֵשׁ כׇּל ״אֵת״ וָ״אֵת״ שֶׁבַּתּוֹרָה, כֵּיוָן שֶׁהִגִּיעַ לְ״אֶת ה׳ אֱלֹהֶיךָ תִּירָא״ פֵּירַשׁ. אָמְרוּ לוֹ תַּלְמִידָיו: רַבִּי, כׇּל ״אֶתִּין״ שֶׁדָּרַשְׁתָּ מָה תְּהֵא עֲלֵיהֶם? אָמַר לָהֶם: כְּשֵׁם שֶׁקִּבׇּלְתִּי שָׂכָר עַל הַדְּרִישָׁה, כָּךְ אֲנִי מְקַבֵּל שָׂכָר עַל הַפְּרִישָׁה.

b5.he: עַד שֶׁבָּא רַבִּי עֲקִיבָא וְלִימֵּד: ״אֶת ה׳ אֱלֹהֶיךָ תִּירָא״ — לְרַבּוֹת תַּלְמִידֵי חֲכָמִים.

b6.he: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב אַחָא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרָבָא לְרַב אָשֵׁי: אֶלָּא מֵעַתָּה, טַעְמָא דְרַבָּנַן מִ״גָּמָל״ ״גָּמָל״, וְרַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן מֵ״אֶת הַגָּמָל״, הָא לָאו הָכִי הֲוָה אָמֵינָא חָלָב דִּבְהֵמָה טְמֵאָה שְׁרֵי?

b7.he: מַאי שְׁנָא מֵהָא דְּתַנְיָא: ״הַטְּמֵאִים״ — לֶאֱסוֹר צִירָן, וְרוֹטְבָן, וְקֵיפֶה שֶׁלָּהֶן?

b8.he: אִיצְטְרִיךְ, סָלְקָא דַּעְתָּךְ אָמֵינָא: הוֹאִיל דִּבְהֵמָה טְהוֹרָה נָמֵי חִידּוּשׁ הוּא, דְּאָמַר מַר: דָּם נֶעְכָּר וְנַעֲשֶׂה חָלָב, וְכֵיוָן דְּחִידּוּשׁ הוּא — בִּבְהֵמָה טְמֵאָה נָמֵי לִישְׁתְּרֵי, קָא מַשְׁמַע לַן.

b9.he: הָנִיחָא לְמַאן דְּאָמַר דָּם נֶעְכָּר וְנַעֲשֶׂה חָלָב, אֶלָּא לְמַאן דְּאָמַר אֵיבָרֶיהָ מִתְפָּרְקִין הֵימֶנָּה וְאֵין נַפְשָׁהּ חוֹזֶרֶת עָלֶיהָ עַד עֶשְׂרִים וְאַרְבָּעָה חֹדֶשׁ, מַאי אִיכָּא לְמֵימַר?

b10.he: אִיצְטְרִיךְ, סָלְקָא דַּעְתָּךְ אָמֵינָא: הוֹאִיל וְלֵיכָּא מִידֵּי דְּאָתֵי מֵחַי וְשַׁרְיֵיהּ רַחֲמָנָא, וְהַאי חָלָב כִּי אֵבֶר מִן הַחַי הוּא, וּשְׁרֵי, וְהִילְכָּךְ אֲפִילּוּ בִּבְהֵמָה טְמֵאָה לִישְׁתְּרֵי, קָא מַשְׁמַע לַן.

b11.he: וְחָלָב דִּבְהֵמָה טְהוֹרָה מְנָלַן דִּשְׁרֵי? אִילֵימָא מִדַּאֲסַר רַחֲמָנָא ״בָּשָׂר בְּחָלָב״, הָא לְחוּדֵיהּ שְׁרֵי, וְאֵימָא: חָלָב לְחוּדֵיהּ אָסוּר בַּאֲכִילָה וּמוּתָּר בַּהֲנָאָה, בָּשָׂר בְּחָלָב — בַּהֲנָאָה נָמֵי אָסוּר!

b12.he: וּלְרַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן, דְּשָׁרֵי בַּהֲנָאָה, מַשְׁכַּחַתְּ לַהּ לְמִילְקֵי עַל בִּישּׁוּלֵיהּ!

b13.he: אֶלָּא מִדְּגַלִּי רַחֲמָנָא דְּבִפְסוּלֵי הַמּוּקְדָּשִׁין, ״תִּזְבַּח״ — וְלֹא גִּיזָּה, ״בָּשָׂר״ — וְלֹא חָלָב, הָא דְּחוּלִּין שְׁרֵי.

b14.he: וְאֵימָא: דְּחוּלִּין אָסוּר בַּאֲכִילָה וּשְׁרֵי בַּהֲנָאָה, דְּקָדָשִׁים בַּהֲנָאָה נָמֵי אָסוּר!

b15.he: אֶלָּא, מִדִּכְתִיב: ״וְדֵי חֲלֵב עִזִּים לְלַחְמְךָ לְלֶחֶם בֵּיתֶךָ וְחַיִּים לְנַעֲרוֹתֶיךָ״.

b16.he: וְדִילְמָא לִסְחוֹרָה? אֶלָּא מִדִּכְתִיב ״וְאֵת עֲשֶׂרֶת חֲרִיצֵי הֶחָלָב״.

b17.he: וְדִלְמָא לִסְחוֹרָה? אַטּוּ דַּרְכָּהּ שֶׁל מִלְחָמָה לִסְחוֹרָה?!

b18.he: וְאִיבָּעֵית אֵימָא מֵהָכָא: ״אֶרֶץ זָבַת חָלָב וּדְבָשׁ״, וְאִי לָא דִּשְׁרֵי, מִשְׁתַּבַּח לַן קְרָא בְּמִידֵּי דְּלָא חֲזֵי? וְאִיבָּעֵית אֵימָא מֵהָכָא: ״לְכוּ שִׁבְרוּ וֶאֱכֹלוּ, וּלְכוּ שִׁבְרוּ בְּלֹא כֶסֶף וּבְלֹא מְחִיר יַיִן וְחָלָב״.

b20.he: אֶלָּא לְכִדְתַנְיָא: לָמָּה נִשְׁנוּ בַּבְּהֵמָה — מִפְּנֵי ״הַשְּׁסוּעָה״, וּבָעוֹפוֹת — מִפְּנֵי ״הָרָאָה״.

b21.he: ״גָּמָל״ ״גָּמָל״ נָמֵי לְהָכִי הוּא דַּאֲתָא! כֹּל הֵיכָא דְּאִיכָּא לְמִידְרָשׁ דָּרְשִׁינַן.

b22.he: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: רָחֵל שֶׁיָּלְדָה מִין עֵז, וְעֵז שֶׁיָּלְדָה מִין רָחֵל — פְּטוּרָה מִן הַבְּכוֹרָה, וְאִם יֵשׁ בּוֹ מִקְצָת סִימָנִים — חַיֶּיבֶת. רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן אוֹמֵר: עַד שֶׁיְּהֵא רֹאשׁוֹ וְרוּבּוֹ דּוֹמֶה לְאִמּוֹ.

b23.he: אִיבַּעְיָא לְהוּ: לַאֲכִילָה, מִי בָּעֵי רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן רֹאשׁוֹ וְרוּבּוֹ, אוֹ לָא?

b24.he: לְעִנְיַן בְּכוֹרָה, כְּתִיב: ״אַךְ בְּכוֹר שׁוֹר״, עַד שֶׁיְּהֵא הוּא שׁוֹר וּבְכוֹרוֹ שׁוֹר. אֲבָל לַאֲכִילָה, גָּמָל הוּא דְּאָמַר רַחֲמָנָא דַּאֲסִיר, הָא

messages.text: 6a

Continued from 5b: in a baraita, Rabbi Yosei HaGelili says “the firstborn of non-kosher animals you shall redeem” would include horses and camels, and “firstborn of a donkey” limits it to donkeys. Still, one might say that only donkeys are redeemed with a lamb, and horses and camels with any item.

Therefore, the verse states the phrase: “Firstborn of a donkey” (Exodus 13:13), “firstborn of a donkey” (Exodus 34:20), mentioning it a total of two times. The additional usage of the term indicates I said to you that firstborn status applies only to firstborns of donkeys, but not to firstborns of horses or camels.

verse.he: וּפֶטֶר חֲמוֹר תִּפְדֶּה בְשֶׂה וְאִם־לֹא תִפְדֶּה וַעֲרַפְתּוֹ כֹּל בְּכוֹר בָּנֶיךָ תִּפְדֶּה וְלֹא־יֵרָאוּ פָנַי רֵיקָם׃
verse.en:
But the firstling of a donkey you shall redeem with a sheep; if you do not redeem it, you must break its neck. And you must redeem every male first-born among your children.
None shall appear before Me empty-handed.

notes.he: מקרא אחר (שמות ל״ד:כ׳) ופטר חמור תפדה בשה אם אינו ענין למעט שאר בהמה טמאה משה שהרי מעטן בפסוק ראשון תנהו ענין למעטן מכל קדושת בכור:
notes.en: The verse states: another verse (Exodus 34:20), “And the firstborn of a donkey you shall redeem with a lamb.” If it is not needed to exclude the other non-kosher animals from [redemption with] a lamb, since the first verse already excluded them, apply it to excluding them from all firstborn sanctity.

messages.text: How can the extra verse alone indicate that other firstborn non-kosher animals do not have firstborn status? If the Merciful One had written the term “firstborn of a donkey” once, I would say a firstborn donkey is an item that was included in a generalization of all non-kosher animals, but emerged from the generalization to teach that it must be redeemed by means of a lamb.

notes.he: הא תרוייהו צריכי דאי כתב חד הוה אמינא הוי פטר חמור דבר שהיה בכלל בכור הבהמה הטמאה תפדה:
notes.en: Rav Aḥa refutes [Rashi reads “Rav Aḥa”; the daf and the Davidson English read “Rav Aḥai”]: but both of them are needed, for had it written one, I would say the firstborn of a donkey is an item that was included in the generalization “the firstborn of the non-kosher animal you shall redeem.”

notes.he: היכי מצית למעט פיטרי סוסים וגמלים מכל דבר דהא פטר חמור אחרינא לא מייתי להכי אלא תרוייהו צריכי:
notes.en: Rav Aḥai challenges: how can you exclude firstborn horses and camels from everything, when the other “firstborn of a donkey” does not come for that? Rather, both are needed.

notes.he: דאי כתב רחמנא חד הוה אמינא הוה פטר חמור דבר שהיה בכלל בכור הבהמה הטמאה תפדה:
notes.en: For had the Merciful One written one, I would say the firstborn of a donkey was an item included in the generalization “the firstborn of the non-kosher animal you shall redeem.”

messages.text: According to the principles of exegesis, it emerged from the generalization to teach not just about itself, but emerged to teach about the entire generalization. And accordingly, all non-kosher animals should actually be redeemed by means of a lamb as well.

notes.he: שפדיונו בשה לא ללמד על עצמו יצא אלא ללמד על הכלל כולו יצא כו' ולעולם נפדין בשה ת"ל מקרא אחר ופטר חמור תפדה לומר לך זה בשה ולא אחר בשה:
notes.en: And emerged from the generalization to teach: that its redemption is with a lamb. It emerged not to teach about itself alone but to teach about the entire generalization, etc., and actually they are all redeemed with a lamb. Therefore the verse states another verse, “And the firstborn of a donkey you shall redeem,” to tell you: this one with a lamb, and no other with a lamb.

notes.he: דכתב ופטר חמור תפדה בשה ולא ללמד על עצמו כו':
notes.en: And emerged from the generalization: since it wrote “and the firstborn of a donkey you shall redeem with a lamb,” and not to teach about itself, etc.

messages.text: Therefore, the Merciful One writes: “Firstborn of a donkey,” another time, to teach that only firstborn donkeys must be redeemed by means of a lamb, but not firstborn horses or camels.

And therefore I can say that perhaps the earlier suggestion is correct: The Torah excluded firstborn horses and camels from being redeemed by means of a lamb, but actually, they must still be redeemed by means of any other item.

notes.he: וקדושים בבכור:
notes.en: He excluded them from a lamb, but actually with any item: and they are sanctified as firstborn.

messages.text: If it is so that the Torah excludes horses and camels only from redemption by means of a lamb but not from redemption in general, let the Merciful One write: Firstborn of a donkey you shall redeem with a lamb, and: A donkey you shall redeem with a lamb, which would suffice.
messages.quote: but actually, they must still be redeemed by means of any other item

notes.he: קרא תניינא חמור בשה תפדה ואנא ידענא דבפטר קמישתעי מדהדר כתב פטר ש"מ מדין פטר רחם ממעט להו לשאר בהמות טמאות דאין להם דין בכורה:
notes.en: If so, let it write: in the second verse, “a donkey you shall redeem with a lamb,” and I would know that it speaks of a firstborn. Since it wrote “firstborn” again, learn from it that it excludes the other non-kosher animals from the law of “opening the womb”: they have no law of the firstborn.

messages.text: Why do I need the verse to state: “A firstborn of a donkey you shall redeem with a lamb,” “a firstborn of a donkey you shall redeem with a lamb,” using the same phrase both times? It is necessary to teach that I said to you that firstborn status applies only to firstborns of donkeys, but not to firstborns of horses or camels.

notes.he: דלעולם בכל דבר א"כ לכתוב ופטר חמור תפדה בשה וחמור תפדה בשה פטר פטר תרי זימני למה לי פטרי חמור אמרתי לך לפדות ולא פטרי סוסים וגמלים כו':
notes.en: If so: that actually they are redeemed with any item, then let it write “and the firstborn of a donkey you shall redeem with a lamb” and “and a donkey you shall redeem with a lamb.” Why do I need “firstborn,” “firstborn,” twice? [To teach:] I told you to redeem firstborn donkeys, and not firstborn horses and camels, etc.

messages.text: And as for the tanna of our mishna, who derived from the repetition of the phrase “firstborn of a donkey” that the mitzva of redeeming a firstborn donkey applies only if the mother and offspring are both donkeys, from where does he derive that the Torah excludes horses and camels from firstborn status?

It is derived from the verse: “From all your livestock you shall take the males, the firstborn of the ox and lamb. And the firstborn of a donkey you shall redeem with a lamb” (Exodus 34:19–20). The phrase “From all your livestock you shall take the males” is a generalization, and the reference to an ox and a lamb and a donkey is a detail.

verse.he: כׇּל־פֶּטֶר רֶחֶם לִי וְכׇל־מִקְנְךָ תִּזָּכָר פֶּטֶר שׁוֹר וָשֶׂה׃ וּפֶטֶר חֲמוֹר תִּפְדֶּה בְשֶׂה וְאִם־לֹא תִפְדֶּה וַעֲרַפְתּוֹ כֹּל בְּכוֹר בָּנֶיךָ תִּפְדֶּה וְלֹא־יֵרָאוּ פָנַי רֵיקָם׃
verse.en:
Every first issue of the womb is Mine, from all your livestock that drop a male, form uncertain. as firstling, whether cattle or sheep. But the firstling of a donkey you shall redeem with a sheep; if you do not redeem it, you must break its neck. And you must redeem every male first-born among your children.
None shall appear before Me empty-handed.

notes.he: פטר שור ושה ופטר חמור תפדה בשה כלל ופרט בהדדי:
notes.en: “All your livestock … that is male”: “the firstborn of an ox and a lamb,” and “the firstborn of a donkey you shall redeem with a lamb.” A generalization and a detail next to each other.

notes.he: כל מקנך תזכר כלל שור ושה וחמור דסמיך ליה ופטר חמור תפדה בשה וחשיב ליה בפרטא:
notes.en: “All your livestock that is male” is a generalization; ox and lamb, and the donkey that is adjacent to it, “and the firstborn of a donkey you shall redeem with a lamb,” he counts in the detail.

messages.text: According to the principles of exegesis, in the case of a generalization and a detail, the generalization is referring only to that which is specified in the detail. Therefore, an ox and a lamb and a donkey, yes, their offspring have firstborn status, but anything else, no, it does not have firstborn status.

And as for Rabbi Yosei HaGelili, how does he respond to this claim? He holds that a donkey is not included in the generalization “From all your livestock you shall take the males,” as the word “firstborn” in the phrase “and the firstborn of a donkey,” indicates that the Torah interrupts the matter, i.e., the list of details.
messages.quote: an ox and a lamb and a donkey is a detail

notes.he: דלא תדייניה בכלל ופרט דאי אקרא קמא קא מהדר מכדי כתיב לעיל מיניה פטר שור ושה לכתוב וחמור תפדה בשה ונהדר אפטר דלעיל אלא מדהדר כתב פטר ש"מ לאו אקרא קמא קמהדר:
notes.en: “Firstborn” of a donkey interrupts the matter: so that you should not judge it by the generalization and the detail. For if it were going back to the first verse, consider: “the firstborn of an ox and a lamb” is written just before it, so let it write “and a donkey you shall redeem with a lamb,” and it would refer back to the “firstborn” above. Since it wrote “firstborn” again, learn from it that it is not going back to the first verse.

notes.he: אמר לך האי חמור לא הוי מפרטא דפטר הפסיק הענין ואי אתה לדונו לחמור עם שור ושה בכלל ופרט ולאו כלל ופרט הוא:
notes.en: And Rabbi Yosei HaGelili would tell you: this donkey is not part of the detail, since “firstborn” interrupts the matter, and you cannot judge the donkey together with the ox and the lamb by generalization and detail; it is not a generalization and detail.

messages.text: And as for the Rabbis, how do they respond to this claim? The letter vav, meaning “and,” in the phrase “and the firstborn of a donkey,” indicates that the verse returns and combines the donkey with the other animals as having firstborn status.

notes.he: דכתב ופטר הדר ערביה ואהדריה אקרא קמא דוי"ו מוסף על ענין ראשון:
notes.en: Vav: since it wrote “and the firstborn,” it combined it again and brought it back to the first verse, for a vav adds to the preceding matter.

notes.he: ורבנן אמרי אין ודאי חמור נמי הוי מההוא פרטא דוי"ו ופטר הדר וערביה דמוסף על ענין ראשון והוי נמי מפרטא:
notes.en: And the Rabbis say: yes, certainly the donkey too is part of that detail, since the vav of “and the firstborn” combines it again, adding to the first matter, and it is also part of the detail.

messages.text: And as for Rabbi Yosei HaGelili, how does he respond? He holds that if the donkey was indeed included in the delineation of the other animals that follows the generalization, the Torah would write neither the letter vav nor the word “firstborn,” and it still would be included.

notes.he: אמר לך אי אקרא קמא קאי לא לכתוב פטר לאפסוקיה ולא נצטרך וי"ו לערביה:
notes.en: And Rabbi Yosei would tell you: if it were going back to the first verse, it should not have written “firstborn” to interrupt it, and then it would not need a vav to combine it.

notes.he: א"כ דחד פרטא הוא לא לכתוב לא וי"ו ולא פטר:
notes.en: And Rabbi Yosei HaGelili: if so, that it is one detail, it should write neither vav nor “firstborn.”

messages.text: And as for the Rabbis, how do they respond to this claim? Since this, a firstborn donkey, has sanctity that inheres in its value and must be redeemed by means of a lamb, and that, a firstborn ox and lamb, possess inherent sanctity and are sacrificed upon the altar, the word “firstborn” must interpose between them, and the verse must combine them again with the letter vav for “and,” which indicates that a donkey is also included in the delineation that defines the generalization “From all your livestock you shall take the males.”

notes.he: למימר דלידייניה בכלל ופרט:
notes.en: And it combines them again: to say that it should be judged by the generalization and the detail.

notes.he: ופטר והדר ו' ועריב להו דהוו חד פרטא ור' יוסי לא משמע ליה האי והדר עריב:
notes.en: It interrupts it: with “and the firstborn,” and then the vav combines them, so that they are one detail. And Rabbi Yosei does not accept this “and then it combines.”

messages.text: The Gemara previously cited the mishna (16b) that rules that a ewe that gave birth to a goat of sorts and a goat that gave birth to a ewe of sorts are exempt from the mitzva of the firstborn. And if the offspring has some of the characteristics of its mother, it is subject to the obligations of firstborn status.

In the case of a cow that gave birth to a donkey of sorts, where the mishna (5b) ruled that the offspring does not have firstborn status, and it has some of the characteristics of the mother, what is the halakha?
messages.lead: A dilemma was raised before the Sages about a related matter:

notes.he: שדומה לפרה:
notes.en: And it has some of the characteristics: that it resembles a cow.

messages.text: When the mishna states with regard to a goat that gave birth to a ewe of sorts and a ewe that gave birth to a goat of sorts, that when it has some of the characteristics of the mother, it is obligated, i.e., subject to the obligations of firstborn status, perhaps this is because a ewe and a goat are somewhat similar; as this one is a kosher animal and that one is a kosher animal. Likewise, this one has inherent sanctity and may be sacrificed on the altar, and that one has inherent sanctity.

But here, in the case of a cow that gave birth to a donkey of sorts, perhaps the halakha would be different, as this, the offspring, resembles a non-kosher animal, and that, the mother, is a kosher animal. Likewise, the firstborns of this species, the cow, possess inherent sanctity, and the firstborns of that species, the donkey, have sanctity that inheres in its value. Therefore, perhaps the offspring does not have firstborn status, even if it has some of the characteristics of the mother.
Or perhaps it can be reasoned that since both this cow and that donkey are sanctified with firstborn status, the offspring is sanctified with firstborn status.

And if you say that since both this cow and that donkey are sanctified with firstborn status, the offspring is also sanctified with firstborn status if it has some characteristics of the mother, then what is the halakha in a case of a donkey that gave birth to a horse of sorts? Perhaps here the offspring certainly does not have firstborn status, as a horse is not sanctified with firstborn status.

Or perhaps one can reason that since the mother is a member of a non-kosher species, as is the offspring, the offspring should be sanctified with firstborn status, as it has some characteristics of the mother, which is a donkey.

notes.he: דתרוייהו שוו דמין בהמה טמאה נינהו לאו שינויא יתירא הוא וכי אית מקצת סימנים דאם חייב:
notes.en: Or perhaps, since: both of them are alike in being of a non-kosher animal species, it is not a great change, and when it has some of the characteristics, [the mother] is obligated.

notes.he: או דלמא כיון דמין טמאה הוא האם והבן והאם קדוש בבכורה קדוש גם הבן הואיל ויש בו מקצת סימן:
notes.en: Or perhaps, since the mother and the offspring are of a non-kosher species, and the mother is sanctified as a firstborn, the offspring too is sanctified, since it has some of the characteristics.

messages.text: If you say in the previous case that since it is a non-kosher species it is sanctified, then what is the halakha in the case of a cow that gave birth to a horse of sorts? Here, one can say there certainly is no reason for the offspring to have firstborn status, as this cow is kosher and that horse is non-kosher. And in addition, this cow is sanctified with firstborn status and that horse is not sanctified with firstborn status.
Or perhaps one can reason that having some of the characteristics of the mother is a significant matter and the offspring does have firstborn sanctity.

notes.he: חשובה היא דאע"ג דאישתני כולי האי מחייבי ליה מקצת סימנין בבכורה:
notes.en: Characteristics are a matter: of importance. Even though it has changed so much, some of the characteristics make it subject to firstborn status.

messages.caption: An offspring with some of its mother’s features: the starting point and the three dilemmas, and what 6a resolves.

messages.text: Come and hear a proof from a baraita:

A kosher animal that gave birth to a non-kosher animal of sorts is exempt from its offspring being counted a firstborn. If the offspring has some of the characteristics of the mother it is obligated, i.e., subject to the obligations of firstborn status.
What, does this not include even the case of a cow that gave birth to a horse of sorts?
messages.quote: A kosher animal that gave birth to a non-kosher animal of sorts

notes.dh: מאי לאו אפי' פרה שילדה מין סוס
notes.he: וש"מ סימנא מילתא היא וכ"ש כולהו אינך:
notes.en: What, is it not even a cow that gave birth to a horse of sorts: and learn from it that characteristics are a significant matter, and all the more so in all the other cases.

messages.text: No, it is referring to a case such as where a cow that gave birth to a donkey of sorts, where both species are subject to the sanctity of the firstborn.

notes.he: דהואיל ותרוייהו בני קדושת בהמה נינהו כי אית מקצת סימנין חייב ולא תפשוט מינה אלא חדא:
notes.en: No, a cow that gave birth to a donkey of sorts: since both are of species subject to the sanctity of the [firstborn] animal, when it has some of the characteristics it is obligated. And you can resolve only one [dilemma] from it.

notes.he: כי יש בו מקצת סימן א' חייב דאידי ואידי בני מיקדש בכורה נינהו ובהא קאמר ברייתא בהמה טהורה שילדה מין טמאה ולא שילדה מין סוס ואכתי לא ידעינן לא בחמור שילדה מין סוס ולא בפרה שילדה מין סוס:
notes.en: No, a cow that gave birth to a donkey of sorts: when it has some of the characteristics, it is obligated, since both are of species that are sanctified as firstborn. It is of this that the baraita says “a kosher animal that gave birth to a non-kosher species,” and not of one that gave birth to a horse of sorts. And we still do not know about a donkey that gave birth to a horse of sorts or about a cow that gave birth to a horse of sorts.

messages.text: Come and hear another proof from a baraita:

In the case of a cow that gave birth to a donkey of sorts or a donkey that gave birth to a horse of sorts, each of the mothers is exempt from their offspring being counted a firstborn. If the offspring has some of the characteristics of the mother, it is obligated, i.e., subject to the obligations of firstborn status.
What, is the last clause not referring to both cases of the baraita? If so, this resolves two of the dilemmas about offspring that have some characteristics of the mother.
messages.quote: If the offspring has some of the characteristics of the mother, it is obligated

notes.he: קאי האי ואם יש מקצת סימנין ותפשוט מינה תרתי:
notes.en: What, is it not both: does this clause, “and if it has some of the characteristics,” not refer to both, and you can resolve two from it?

notes.he: אתרוייהו (קמ"ל) קאי האי אם יש בו מקצת סימנין וש"מ דפרה דילדה מין סוס דחייב בבכורה:
notes.en: What, is it not: this “if it has some of the characteristics” refers to both, and learn from it that a cow that gave birth to a horse of sorts is obligated in firstborn status [so the text; the baraita’s second case is a donkey that gave birth to a horse of sorts].

messages.text: No, it is referring only to the case of a cow that gave birth to a donkey of sorts, so only that dilemma is resolved.

notes.he: ומשום דתרוייהו קדשי בכורות:
notes.en: No, a cow that gave birth to a donkey of sorts: because both are sanctified as firstborns.

notes.he: אפרה שילדה מין חמור קאי:
notes.en: No, it refers to a cow that gave birth to a donkey of sorts.

messages.text: But if so, for what purpose does the baraita teach the case of a donkey that gave birth to a horse of sorts? If it is to exempt the offspring from being accounted firstborn status when it does not have some of the characteristics of its mother, that halakha is obvious for the following reason:
messages.quote: or a donkey that gave birth to a horse of sorts

notes.dh: אבל חמור שילדה מין סוס למאי הלכתא קתני לה הכא לפטורא
notes.he: לאשמעינן דנדמה הוי ופטור מן הבכורה כי לית ביה מקצת סימנין דמשום רישא קתני חמור שילדה מין סוס אבל סיפא לאו עלה מהדר:
notes.en: But a donkey that gave birth to a horse of sorts, for what halakha does it teach it here? To exempt: to teach us that it counts as a different-looking offspring and is exempt from firstborn status when it has none of the characteristics. For it teaches “a donkey that gave birth to a horse of sorts” for the sake of the first clause, but the last clause does not go back to it.

notes.he: דפטורה מן הבכורה כי אין בו מקצת סימנים ואפילו בסימנים פשיטא השתא ומה פרה וכו':
notes.en: For what does it teach it, to exempt: that it is exempt from firstborn status when it has none of the characteristics? And even with the characteristics it is obvious: now, if a cow, etc.

messages.text: And now, if in the case of a cow that gave birth to a donkey of sorts, where both this species and that species are sanctified with firstborn status, you said that if the offspring has some of the characteristics of its mother then yes, it has firstborn status, and if it does not have such characteristics, then no, the offspring does not have firstborn status, then in the case of a donkey that gave birth to a horse of sorts, which generally is not sanctified with firstborn status, is it necessary to state that the horse does not have firstborn status unless it has some of the characteristics of its mother?

It was necessary to teach that case in addition to that of a cow that gave birth to a donkey of sorts, as it might enter your mind that there, in the case of the cow that gave birth to a donkey of sorts, the offspring does not have firstborn status because a cow and donkey are entirely different from one another, as a cow has horns, and this animal, a donkey, does not have horns. Moreover, with regard to that animal, a cow, its hooves are split, but with regard to this animal, a donkey, its hooves are closed [kelutot].

notes.he: חמור שילדה מין סוס דכי אין בו מקצת סימנין מבעיא דפטור אלא לאו אתרויהו קאי וש"מ דחמור דילדה מין סוס דחייב דכי יש בו מקצת סימנים. לעולם אפרה קאי ולא אחמור ואי אמרת א"כ חמור שילדה מין סוס למאי קתני לה לפטור פשיטא לאו פשיט' היא דאיצטר' למיתני לה לפטורה דלא ילפינן לה מפרה שילדה חמור דסד"א התם הוא בפרה שילדה חמור דכי אין לה מקצת סימנים דפטורה דהא יש לה קרנים וכו':
notes.en: A donkey that gave birth to a horse of sorts: when it has none of the characteristics, need it be said that it is exempt? Rather, does it not refer to both, and learn from it that a donkey that gave birth to a horse of sorts is obligated when it has some of the characteristics? Actually, it refers to the cow and not to the donkey. And if you say: if so, for what does it teach a donkey that gave birth to a horse of sorts, to exempt? That is obvious! It is not obvious: it was necessary to teach it, to exempt, because we would not derive it from a cow that gave birth to a donkey, since it might enter your mind that there, with a cow that gave birth to a donkey, it is exempt when it does not have some of the characteristics, because [the cow] has horns, etc.

messages.text: But here, in the case of a donkey that gave birth to a horse of sorts, where a similarity does exist between the mother and its offspring, as this one and that one both do not have horns, and with regard to both this one and that one its hooves are closed, I can say that this offspring is merely a red donkey, i.e., a donkey with the coloring of a horse, and has firstborn status. Therefore, the tanna teaches us that it is a different species from that of the mother, and does not have firstborn status.

notes.he: וליחייב בבכורה קמ"ל. סתם סוסים אדומים הן:
notes.en: A red donkey: and it should be obligated in firstborn status; [the baraita] teaches us [otherwise]. Ordinary horses are red.

notes.he: בחמור שילדה מין סוס דאידי ואידי אין לה קרנים אידי ואידי פרסותי' קלוטות ממאי דהאי מין סוס דלמא לאו סוס הוא אלא חמור אדום בעלמא הוא. דסתם סוס אדום וחמור שחור. והאי דלמא אע"ג דאדום הוא אימא חמור אדום הוא וליחייב בבכור להכי אצטריך למתני לה לפטורה ואכתי לא ילפינן דליחייב בבכור כי יש בו מקצת סימן אלא בפרה שילדה מין חמור אבל חמור שילדה מין סוס ופרה שילדה מין סוס אכתי לא ידעינן:
notes.en: But here, with a donkey that gave birth to a horse of sorts, where neither has horns and both have closed hooves, how do we know that this is a horse of sorts? Perhaps it is not a horse at all but merely a red donkey, for ordinary horses are red and donkeys black. Perhaps this one, though it is red, is a red donkey, and it should be obligated as a firstborn. That is why it needed to teach it, to exempt. And still we learn that it is obligated as a firstborn when it has some of the characteristics only for a cow that gave birth to a donkey of sorts; about a donkey that gave birth to a horse of sorts and a cow that gave birth to a horse of sorts we still do not know.

messages.text: And what is the offspring’s halakhic status with regard to its consumption? In the case of a kosher animal that gave birth to a non-kosher animal of sorts, its consumption is permitted. And in the case of a non-kosher animal that gave birth to a kosher animal of sorts, its consumption is prohibited. This is because that which emerges from the non-kosher animal is non-kosher and that which emerges from the kosher animal is kosher.
messages.lead: § The mishna teaches with regard to an animal whose offspring resembles a different species:

notes.he: מה הוא מיושב יותר שלא דבר אלא בפרה שילדה מין חמור ולא חמור (הילד פרה):
notes.en: And what is their status with regard to eating: [the reading] “what is its status” is smoother, since [the question of eating] concerns only a cow that gave birth to a donkey of sorts, and not a donkey [that gave birth to a horse of sorts, where mother and offspring are both non-kosher]. [The printed text adds here, in parentheses, “the offspring a cow.”]

notes.he: ולדות של בהמה טהורה שהוא כמין בהמה טמאה מותרין הן באכילה שהיוצא מן הטהור טהור והיוצא מן הטמא טמא:
notes.en: And what is their status with regard to eating: the offspring of a kosher animal that look like a non-kosher species are permitted for eating, because what emerges from the kosher is kosher and what emerges from the non-kosher is non-kosher.

messages.text: Why do I need the mishna to teach the concluding phrase: This is because that which emerges from the non-kosher animal is non-kosher and that which emerges from the kosher animal is kosher?
messages.quote: because that which emerges from the non-kosher animal is non-kosher

notes.he: לקמן דייק מינה מי רגלים של חמור אסורין והכא דייק מדקתני שהיוצא שנותן טעם לדבר הוה ליה למיתני והיוצא:
notes.en: Why do I need to teach “because that which emerges”: below, it infers from this that a donkey’s urine is forbidden. And here it infers [the question] from its wording “because that which emerges,” which gives a reason for the matter; it should have taught “and that which emerges.”

messages.text: It is merely a mnemonic to ensure that you do not mistakenly reverse the halakha in these two cases,

notes.he: דלא תחליף לך. גירסתך במשנה ותימא טהורה שילדה מין טמאה אסור וטמאה שילדה מין טהורה מותר:
notes.en: Merely a mnemonic: so that it does not get switched for you. Your recitation of the mishna, so that you do not say: a kosher animal that gave birth to a non-kosher species is forbidden, and a non-kosher animal that gave birth to a kosher species is permitted.

notes.he: לגירס' דלא תיחלף לך איזה מותר באכילה דיכיל איניש למיטעא ביה:
notes.en: It is merely a mnemonic: for the recitation, so that it does not get switched for you which one is permitted for eating, since a person could err in it.

messages.text: so that you do not say: Follow its appearance, and therefore this offspring that looks like a kosher animal is a full-fledged kosher animal, despite being born to a non-kosher animal; and that one that looks like a non-kosher animal is a full-fledged non-kosher animal, despite its mother being a kosher animal. Rather, the mishna teaches that one must follow the status of its mother.

notes.he: דנולד אי הוי מין טהור ליהוי טהור מעליא הלכך קאמר שהיוצא מן הטהור דזיל בתר אימיה אי אימיה טהורה היוצא ממנה אע"ג שהוא מין טמא טהור:
notes.en: So that you do not say, follow its own: [the appearance] of the newborn, so that if it is a kosher species it is fully kosher. Therefore it says “because what emerges from the kosher”: follow its mother. If its mother is kosher, what emerges from her is kosher, even though it is a non-kosher species.

messages.text: From where are these matters derived? They are derived from a verse, as the Sages taught:

When the verse states: “Nevertheless these shall you not eat, of them that chew the cud, or of them that split the hoof” (Leviticus 11:4), this verse indicates that you have an animal that chews the cud and has split hooves, but nevertheless you may not eat it. And which is this? It is a kosher animal that was born from a non-kosher animal.

verse.he: אַךְ אֶת־זֶה לֹא תֹאכְלוּ מִמַּעֲלֵי הַגֵּרָה וּמִמַּפְרִסֵי הַפַּרְסָה אֶת־הַגָּמָל כִּי־מַעֲלֵה גֵרָה הוּא וּפַרְסָה אֵינֶנּוּ מַפְרִיס טָמֵא הוּא לָכֶם׃
verse.en: The following, however, of those that either chew the cud or have true hoofs, you shall not eat: the camel—although it chews the cud, it has no true hoofs: it is impure for you;

messages.text: Or perhaps it excludes only a non-kosher animal that does not chew the cud or have split hooves that was born from a kosher animal, and if so what is the explanation of the verse “of them that chew the cud, or of them that split the hoof”?

notes.he: אפילו טמאה הנולדה מן הטהורה לא תאכלו ומאי ממעלה הגרה כיון דטמא הוא אינו מעלה גרה:
notes.en: Or perhaps: even a non-kosher [offspring] born from a kosher one you shall not eat. And what is [meant by] “of them that chew the cud”? [Born of them;] since it is non-kosher, it does not itself chew the cud.

messages.text: 6b
This is what it is saying: You shall not eat a being that comes from one of those animals that chew their cud and have split hooves if it itself does not have the signs of being kosher.

notes.he: כגון האי טמא שנולד מן הטהורה:
notes.en: A being that comes from those that chew the cud: such as this non-kosher one that was born from a kosher one.

messages.text: To counter this, the continuation of the verse states: “The camel…is impure for you” (Leviticus 11:4). This indicates that a camel itself is non-kosher, but a non-kosher animal that is born from a kosher animal is not non-kosher; rather, it is kosher.

notes.he: וסתם גמלים נולדים מן הגמלה וכתב הוא דמשמע שהוא טמא ואין אחר שהוא גמל טמא וכגון שנולד מן הפרה:
notes.en: The camel, it is impure: ordinary camels are born from a female camel. And it wrote “it,” which implies: it is impure, and no other that is a camel is impure, for example one born from a cow.

notes.he: הכי קאמר דבר הבא וכו' ת"ל ואת הגמל גמל הוא טמא ולא טמא הנולד מן טהורה:
notes.en: This is what it is saying, a being that comes, etc. The verse states: “and the camel … it is impure”; and not an impure one born from a kosher one.

messages.text: It is stated: “Camel” (Leviticus 11:4), “camel” (Deuteronomy 14:7), teaching the term two times with regard to the prohibition of consumption. This teaches that both a camel that is born from a camel and a camel that is born from a cow are non-kosher.

verse.he: אַךְ אֶת־זֶה לֹא תֹאכְלוּ מִמַּעֲלֵי הַגֵּרָה וּמִמַּפְרִיסֵי הַפַּרְסָה הַשְּׁסוּעָה אֶת־הַגָּמָל וְאֶת־הָאַרְנֶבֶת וְאֶת־הַשָּׁפָן כִּי־מַעֲלֵה גֵרָה הֵמָּה וּפַרְסָה לֹא הִפְרִיסוּ טְמֵאִים הֵם לָכֶם׃
verse.en: But the following, which do bring up the cud or have true hoofs that are cleft through, you may not eat: the camel, the hare, and the daman—for although they bring up the cud, they have no true hoofs—they are impure for you;

notes.dh: ר' שמעון אומר גמל גמל ב' פעמים
notes.he: דתורת כהנים ובמשנה תורה אחד לאסור גמל הנולד מן הגמלה ואחד לאסור גמל הנולד מן הפרה. דלא סבירא ליה שהיוצא מן הטהור טהור:
notes.en: Rabbi Shimon says, camel, camel, twice: in Torat Kohanim and in Mishneh Torah; one to prohibit a camel born from a female camel and one to prohibit a camel born from a cow. For he does not hold that what emerges from the kosher is kosher.

messages.text: According to Rabbi Shimon, a non-kosher animal born to a kosher animal is forbidden for consumption, in contrast to the ruling in the mishna.

And as for the Rabbis in the baraita, who disagree with Rabbi Shimon, what do they do with this repetition of “camel,” “camel”? One of the verses is written to prohibit the camel itself and one is written to prohibit the female camel’s milk.

notes.he: אחד בתורת כהנים ואחד במשנה תורה:
notes.en: Camel, camel: one in Torat Kohanim [Leviticus] and one in Mishneh Torah [Deuteronomy].

notes.he: של גמלה:
notes.en: To prohibit its milk: of the female camel.

notes.he: דסברי שהיוצא מן הטהור טהור גמל גמל מאי עבדי ליה חד לגמל עצמו ואידך גמל לאסור חלבו:
notes.en: And the Rabbis, who hold that what emerges from the kosher is kosher, what do they do with “camel, camel”? One for the camel itself, and the other “camel” to prohibit its milk.

messages.text: And as for Rabbi Shimon, from where does he derive that a camel’s milk is forbidden? He derives it from the phrase “the camel [et hagamal].” The verse could have stated just the term “hagamal.” The addition of the word “et” teaches that the prohibition applies also to its milk.

notes.he: משמע את הטפל לגמל והיינו חלבו:
notes.en: “Et hagamal”: implies what is secondary to the camel, and that is its milk.

notes.he: הכא דריש ר"ש את ובפ' קמא דמנחות (דף יא:) גבי לבונה אמר ר"ש את לא דריש וצ"ל את לא דריש לההיא דרשא תדע מדלא מייתי עלה ההיא דשמעון העמסוני כדמייתי הכא וא"ת דמשמע הכא מאן דדריש את אסר קלוט כר"ש ורבי יוסי הגלילי דריש בפ' ארבעה וחמשה (ב"ק מא:) דדריש בעל השור נקי מדמי ולדות ואת להנאת עורו ובפ' בהמה המקשה (חולין דף ע:) שרי קלוט גבי בהמה שמת עוברה ואמר ר' יוסי הגלילי בטמאה טמא בטהורה טהור דכתיב וכל הולך על כפיו מהלכי כפים טמא לך ופריך קלוט במעי קלוטה ליטמא ש"מ פשיטא לי' לר' יוסי בטהורה טהור וי"ל ניחא ליישב מילתיה דר' יוסי אפילו למ"ד קלוט שרי א"נ בראשו ורובו דמי לאמו איירי דמודה ר' שמעון דשרי ויש לדקדק מהכא דהכי הלכתא דלא דרשינן את דקיימא לן כרבנן דשרו קלוט כדמוכח פרק בהמה המקשה (חולין עה:) ד הכל מודים בקלוט בן קלוטה בן פקועה שמותר תרתי תמיהי דכירי אינשי ש"מ קלוט שרי ואיכא לאוקמא בראשו ורובו דמי לאמו אם כן נתיר קלוט מהא טעמא ואת יעמיד לאסור חלבו וגמל נשנה מפני שסועה כמו שפן וארנבת כדאמר לקמן וה"נ נימא לר' יוסי הגלילי אבל יש לדקדק מדאמר פרק בנות כותים (נדה דף לז.) נקטינן אין קושי סותר בזיבה ואי משכחת תנא דאמר סותר ר' אליעזר היא והתם (דף לה.) מפרש טעמא דר' אליעזר משום דדריש את ובכתובות פ' הנושא (כתובות דף קג.) דאמר הזהרו בכבוד אמכם וקאמר אשת אב הואי ופריך אשת אב נמי דאורייתא היא את אביך לרבות אשת אביך י"ל ניחא לי' ליישב דברי רבי ככולי עלמא עוד נראה דאין זה ראיה מנדה דמה הוא זקוק לומר אי משכחת תנא דאמר סותר ר' אליעזר היא הא איכא כל הני תנאי דדרשי את:
notes.en: In brief: Here Rabbi Shimon expounds et, yet in Menaḥot 11b, about frankincense, Rabbi Shimon is said not to expound et; Tosafot answer that he does not expound et for that particular exposition, as shown by the Gemara there not citing Shimon HaAmasoni as it does here. They then ask: the sugya here implies that whoever expounds et forbids a kalut [an unkosher-looking offspring of a kosher animal], like Rabbi Shimon; yet Rabbi Yosei HaGelili expounds et (Bava Kamma 41b, “the owner of the ox,” and et for benefit from its hide), and in Ḥullin 70b treats a kalut born of a kosher animal as permitted. Answers: the Gemara there settles his words even for the view that a kalut is permitted; or it speaks of one whose head and most of the body resemble its mother, which Rabbi Shimon too permits. Tosafot infer that the halakha is that et is not expounded, since we rule like the Rabbis that a kalut is permitted (Ḥullin 75b, “a kalut son of a kalut son of a pekua … two wonders”), though that too could be set where head and most of the body resemble the mother; if so, a kalut could be permitted, et could forbid its milk, and the camel could be repeated for the shesua, and so for Rabbi Yosei HaGelili. Against this they cite Nidda 37a and 35a (Rabbi Eliezer expounds et) and Ketubot 103a (“your father” includes your father’s wife), answering that the Gemara there wished to settle Rabbi’s words according to everyone, and that the Nidda passage proves little, since many tannaim expound et. notes.he: ור"ש (אומר) מנ"ל לאסור חלבו מאת הגמל נפקא את הטפל לבשרו:
notes.en: And Rabbi Shimon, from where does he derive the prohibition of its milk? It comes from “et hagamal”: et, what is secondary to its flesh.

messages.text: And the Rabbis do not interpret instances of “et” as a means to derive new halakhot; they consider it to be an ordinary part of the sentence structure and not a source for exegetical exposition.

notes.he: אתים לא דרשי כשמעון העמסוני דפירש שחזר בו מכל האתים שדרש שאינן באין לרבות הואיל ולא מצא מה לרבות לאת ה' אלהיך תירא:
notes.en: And the Rabbis do not expound instances of et, like Shimon HaAmasoni, who withdrew from all the instances of et he had expounded, [holding] that they do not come to include, since he found nothing to include for “et the Lord your God you shall fear.”

messages.text: As it is taught in a baraita:

Shimon HaAmasoni would interpret each and every occurrence of the word “et” in the Torah, deriving additional halakhot with regard to the particular subject matter. Once he reached the verse: “You shall fear the Lord your God” (Deuteronomy 6:13), which is written with the added word “et,” he withdrew from this method of exposition, as whose fear could be an extension of the fear of God?

verse.he: אֶת־יְהֹוָה אֱלֹהֶיךָ תִּירָא וְאֹתוֹ תַעֲבֹד וּבִשְׁמוֹ תִּשָּׁבֵעַ׃
verse.en: Revere only the ETERNAL your God; worship [God] alone; swear only by God’s name.

notes.he: מכל דרשות שדרש דכל אתין באין לרבות וזה אין מה לרבות בו:
notes.en: He withdrew: from all the expositions he had expounded, for every et comes to include, and this one has nothing to include.

notes.he: וא"ת לוקמא בכבוד אב ואם דמשווה כבודן לכבוד המקום קידושין (דף ל:) ולעבור עליו בשני עשה (כדאמר תפילה ושיחה עשה) י"ל דמשמע ליה דומיא מורא של מקום וזה אי אפשר ורבי עקיבא מרבה תלמידי חכמים דתנן (אבות פ"ד מי"ב) מורא רבך כמורא שמים:
notes.en: He withdrew: and if you ask, let him apply it to the honor of father and mother, whose honor [the Torah] equates with the honor of the Omnipresent (Kiddushin 30b), so that one would transgress two positive commandments (as it says, prayer and conversation are a positive commandment) [so the printed text]. One may answer: he understood that it must be similar to the fear of the Omnipresent, and that is impossible. And Rabbi Akiva includes Torah scholars, as we learned (Avot 4:12): the fear of your teacher should be like the fear of Heaven.

messages.text: His students said to him: Our teacher, what will be with all the occurrences of “et” that you interpreted until now?
Just as I received reward for the exposition, so I receive reward for my withdrawal from using this method of exposition.
“You shall fear the Lord your God”; the word “et” in the verse serves to include Torah scholars, i.e., that one is commanded to fear them just as one fears God.
messages.lead: The word “et” in this verse was not explained until Rabbi Akiva came and taught:

messages.text: In any event, Shimon HaAmasoni no longer derived additional halakhot from “et.” The Rabbis follow the conclusion of Shimon HaAmasoni that “et” is not expounded.

@Rav Ashi If that is so, that the reason of the Rabbis for the halakha that a camel’s milk is forbidden is that it is derived from the words “camel,” “camel,” written twice, and Rabbi Shimon derives it from “the camel [et hagamal],” then could it be reasoned that if not for this derivation I would say that milk of a non-kosher animal is permitted?

notes.he: אי לאו טעמא דרבנן דאסירי ליה לחלב בהמה טמאה מגמל גמל ור' שמעון מאת הגמל הו"א דשרי מ"ש מהא דתניא. אלה הטמאים לאסור צירן ומהכא נילף נמי לחלב:
notes.en: But if that is so: were it not for the reasoning of the Rabbis, who forbid the milk of a non-kosher animal from “camel, camel,” and of Rabbi Shimon, from “et hagamal,” would I say it is permitted? How is it different from what is taught: “these are they that are impure,” to prohibit their juice? Let us derive milk from there too.

messages.text: In what way is this case different from that which is taught in a baraita:

The Torah states with regard to the prohibition against eating creeping animals: “These are they that are impure [hateme’im] to you among all the creeping animals” (Leviticus 11:31). The Sages interpret the letter heh in the term “that are impure [hateme’im]” to prohibit their juice that oozes from their body and their gravy that is produced when they are cooked, and sediments of their flesh that congeal at the bottom of the dish when cooked.

verse.he: אֵלֶּה הַטְּמֵאִים לָכֶם בְּכׇל־הַשָּׁרֶץ כׇּל־הַנֹּגֵעַ בָּהֶם בְּמֹתָם יִטְמָא עַד־הָעָרֶב׃
verse.en: Those are for you the impure among all the swarming things; whoever touches them when they are dead shall be impure until evening.

notes.he: אלה הטמאים לכם בכל השרץ ה"א יתירא:
notes.en: Hateme’im: “These are they that are impure to you among all the creeping animals”; the heh is extra.

notes.he: שומן הדג:
notes.en: To prohibit their juice [tziran]: the fat of the fish.

notes.he: ריסוקי בשר וקפלוטות שבשולי קדירה:
notes.en: Kipa: crumbs of meat and the sediment at the bottom of the pot.

notes.he: אי מהטמאים דריש קשה דבהעור והרוטב (חולין קכב:) מוקמינן ליה לעורו כבשרו ובת"כ לא דריש ליה גבי שרצים אלא גבי בהמה טמאה דכתי' טמאים הם לכם ומיהו ע"כ מהטמאים דשרצים דריש כדמוכח פ' העור והרוטב (חולין קכ. ושבשמעתין דהמחה חלב וגמעו דמייתי על הך דרשא דהטמאים ופריך לכתוב רחמנא בשרצים וליתו הנך וליגמרו מיניה משמע דמינה דריש וצ"ל דמה"א יתירא דהטמא דריש עורות שלהם כבשרם שלהן תדע דגבי בהמה דכתב טמא ולא כתב הטמא דריש בת"כ לאסור צירן ורוטבן ומיהו אכתי דריש מן הטמאים פרק העור והרוטב (חולין קכו:) לר ביצת השרץ ולשם פ"ה ה' יתירא נדרשת לאסור צירו ורוטבו ולעורו כבשרו ולביצת השרץ:
notes.en: Hateme’im, to prohibit their juice and their gravy: if it expounds this from “hateme’im,” it is difficult, for in Ḥullin 122b (Ha’or VeHarotev) we use that word for [counting] their hides like their flesh, and Torat Kohanim expounds [juice and gravy] not about creeping animals but about a non-kosher animal, where it is written “they are impure to you.” Yet it must expound it from the “hateme’im” of creeping animals, as is clear in Ḥullin 120a and in our passage about one who melted forbidden fat and swallowed it, where it cites this exposition of hateme’im and asks: let the Merciful One write it about creeping animals, and let those others be derived from them; which implies that it expounds from it. One must say that from the extra heh of “hatame” it expounds their hides being like their flesh. Proof: about an [unkosher] animal, where it writes “tame” and not “hatame,” Torat Kohanim expounds the prohibition of their juice and gravy. Still, in Ḥullin 126b it expounds “hateme’im” for the egg of a creeping animal, and there Rashi explained: the extra heh is expounded to prohibit its juice and gravy, its hide like its flesh, and the egg of the creeping animal.

notes.he: משמע הכא דציר דאורייתא מדפריך מינה מאי שנא חלב מציר ש"מ דרשה גמורה היא ובפרק העור והרוטב (חולין קכ.) נאמר צריכי וקשה דבפרק אין מעמידין (ע"ז מ.) גבי דג טמא מפליג בין מטבל בצירו לגופו ופרק גיד הנשה (חולין צט:) א"ר יהודה ציר דגים רביעית בסאתים ופריך והא א"ר יהודה מין במינו לא בטיל שאני ציר דזיעה בעלמא הוא משמע שהוא מדרבנן וי"ל ציר דגים דרבנן ציר שרצים דאורייתא ואע"ג דבתורת כהנים נמי דרשי' שקץ הוא לכם גבי דגים אסמכתא בעלמא הוא וא"ת בפרק כל הבשר (חולין קיב:) גבי רב מרי דאמלח בשר שחוטה בהדי טריפה ואסר ליה רבא מהטמאים ופריך ליה מדג טהור שמלחו עם דג טמא היכי פריך מדג לבשר וי"ל דקים ליה דאסור ציר מדרבנן ובמס' תרומות (פ"י מ"ח) נמי תנן ובפ' גיד הנשה (חולין צט:) מייתי לה דג טמא צירו אסור ש"מ הא דשרינן לה משום דלא בלעו ומה שכתוב בספרים ש"מ ציר מותר לא גרס ליה וקצת תימה כיון דצריך קרא בשרץ ובבהמה טמאה ודגים דליכא קרא לא אסר מדאורייתא היכי מייתי רבא ראיה התם מהטמאים לאסור ציר טריפה:
notes.en: In brief: The Gemara challenges from this exposition as a full one, so the juice of creeping animals is forbidden by Torah law (and Ḥullin 120a says both are needed). Yet Avoda Zara 40a distinguishes between dipping in the brine of a non-kosher fish and its body, and Ḥullin 99b (Rabbi Yehuda: fish brine, a revi’it in two se’a; “brine is mere sweat”) implies brine is rabbinic. Answer: fish brine is rabbinic, the juice of creeping animals is from the Torah, and Torat Kohanim’s exposition for fish (“it is an abomination to you”) is a mere support. They ask: in Ḥullin 112b Rava forbade kosher meat salted with treifa meat, citing hateme’im, and was challenged from a kosher fish salted with a non-kosher fish; how can one challenge from fish to meat? Answer: he held fish brine forbidden rabbinically (Terumot 10:8, cited in Ḥullin 99b: “a non-kosher fish, its brine is forbidden”); the kosher fish was permitted only because it did not absorb, and the reading “learn from it that brine is permitted” found in some books should be deleted. A puzzle remains: since a verse is needed for creeping animals, and for a non-kosher animal and fish there is no Torah prohibition without a verse, how did Rava bring proof from hateme’im to forbid the brine of a treifa? notes.he: וא"ת תיפוק לי' ממשרת ליתן טעם כעיקר מכאן אתה דן לכל איסורין שבתורה פסחים (ד' מד.) י"ל עיקר קרא לצירן ואורחא דהש"ס בהכי והתעלמת פעמים שאתה מתעלם ועיקר קרא לזקן ואינו לפי כבודו (ב"מ ד' ל ברכות ד' יט:) ובפ"ק דחגיגה (דף ד.) נמי אמר רגלים פרט לבעלי קבין ואמר פרט לחגר וסומא ולא עיקר קרא לבעלי קבין דמפעמים דריש ליה התם. ומיהו כאן אין צריך לומר כך דאיצטריך לרוטב וקיפה לאשמועי' דהוי כממש אם המחה השרץ דהוי כשתיה ואינו בכלל אכילה ואכילה כתיב בהון קמ"ל בכלל אכילתו והתם (חולין קכ.) מייתי לה גבי המחה חלב חמץ ונבלת עוף טהור וגמעו מיהו קשה דמשמע הכא דאיצטריך לציר לאשמועינן דחשיב כגוף השרץ דפריך מינה אחלב דיתסר כמו ציר וצ"ל דשקולים הן ומיהו מציר לחודיה לא הוה שמעינן דליהוי שתיה כאכילה דהוה מצי לאוקמא כשהקפהו ואכלו:
notes.en: In brief: Why is a verse needed for gravy and sediment, when “steeping” (Pesaḥim 44a) already teaches that taste counts as substance for all the Torah’s prohibitions? Tosafot first answer that the verse is mainly about the juice, and the Talmud often cites a verse for a secondary point (“you shall hide yourself,” whose main point is an elder for whom it is beneath his dignity, Bava Metzia 30a and Berakhot 19b; Ḥagiga 4a on “regalim”). But here that is not needed: the verse teaches that even if one melted the creeping animal, which is drinking rather than eating, it counts as eating it, and Ḥullin 120a cites it for one who melted forbidden fat, leaven or the carcass of a kosher bird and swallowed it. A difficulty: our passage implies the verse is needed for juice, to count it as the creeping animal’s body, since it challenges from it about milk; Tosafot answer that the two are equal, and that from juice alone we would not learn that drinking is like eating, since it could mean juice that congealed and was eaten. Open on Sefaria for the full text.

notes.he: בפ' העור והרוטב (חולין קכ.) אמר מאי קיפה פרמא ופריך הוא עצמו לטמא טומאת אוכלים אלא מאי קיפה תבלין אבל הכא יכול לקרות בין פרמא בין תבלין דלא אתא לאשמועינן אלא שתיהן כאכילה וכן משמע בפ"ה שפירש רסוקי בשר וקפלוט שבשולי קדירה:
notes.en: Their sediment [kipa]: in Ḥullin 120a it says: what is kipa? Chopped meat [parma]. And it asks: that itself imparts the impurity of foods! Rather, what is kipa? Spices. But here one can read it as either chopped meat or spices, since it comes only to teach that drinking them counts as eating. So too Rashi’s commentary implies, for he explained it as crumbs of meat and the sediment at the bottom of the pot.

messages.text: Evidently, any liquid that emerges from a non-kosher animal is forbidden.

The additional exposition to derive that camel’s milk is forbidden was necessary, because it might enter your mind to say it may be permitted, since the permissibility of consumption of the milk of a kosher animal is also a novelty. The milk originates from the blood, which is forbidden for consumption, as the Master said that the reason a nursing woman does not experience menstruation is because the blood is spoiled and becomes milk.
messages.quote: milk of a non-kosher animal is permitted?

notes.he: במסכת נדה (דף ט.) דם נדות נעכר מחמת הלידה ונעשה חלב הלכך חידוש הוא דמעיקרא הוה דם והאוכלו בכרת והשתא מישתרי:
notes.en: As the Master said: in tractate Nidda (9a): the menstrual blood is spoiled because of the birth and becomes milk. Therefore it is a novelty, since at first it was blood, for eating which one is liable to karet, and now it is permitted.

notes.he: למילף מן הגמל סד"א הואיל ובבהמה טהורה הוי חדוש הוא דחלב שרי ומאי חדוש כדאמר מר לגבי מניקה כדאמרינן ד' נשים דיין שעתן דאינן מטמאין למפרע לא מפקידה לפקידה ולא מעת לעת. ואלו הן בתולה ומעוברת מניקה וזקנה משום דאלו אין להן דמים הרבה דמניקה דמה נעכר ונעשה חלב ומשום הכי אינה מטמאה למפרע וכיון דחלב מדם אתי בדין הוא דליתסר גבי בהמה לאכילה אלא דחדוש הוא דשרייה רחמנא כדבעינן למימר לקמן וכיון דחדוש הוא בבהמה טמאה נמי לישתריה להכי איצטריך הגמל לאסור:
notes.en: It was necessary, to derive it from “the camel.” It might enter your mind: since with a kosher animal it is a novelty that milk is permitted. And what is the novelty? As the Master said about a nursing woman, as we say: four women, their time suffices, so that they do not impart impurity retroactively, neither from examination to examination nor for twenty-four hours: a virgin, a pregnant woman, a nursing woman and an old woman, because these do not have much blood. For a nursing woman’s blood is spoiled and becomes milk, and therefore she does not impart impurity retroactively. And since milk comes from blood, by right it should be forbidden for eating in an animal, but it is a novelty that the Merciful One permitted it, as we shall say below. And since it is a novelty, let it be permitted with a non-kosher animal too. That is why “the camel” was needed, to forbid it.

messages.text: Since it is a novelty that the Torah permits milk despite its origins, it might enter your mind to say that with regard to a non-kosher animal it should also be permitted. Therefore, the verse teaches us that it is forbidden.
This works out well according to the one who says that a nursing woman does not menstruate because the blood is spoiled and becomes milk.
messages.quote: the blood is spoiled and becomes milk

notes.he: דמניקה משו"ה דיה שעתה דאינה מטמאה למפרע אלא מכאן ולהבא משום דדם נעכר ונעשה חלב לטעמא דידיה יכלת למימר דחדוש הוא ולהכי איצטריך אידך קרא:
notes.en: This works out well according to the one who says: a nursing woman’s time suffices, so that she imparts impurity only from now on and not retroactively, for this reason: that the blood is spoiled and becomes milk. By his reasoning you can say it is a novelty, and therefore the other verse was needed.

messages.text: But according to the one who says that the milk does not originate from blood, but rather the reason she does not menstruate is because her limbs become disjointed and her soul, i.e., her health, does not return to her until twenty-four months later, what is there to say? Why does the Torah employ a verse to render forbidden the milk of a non-kosher animal?

notes.he: מחמת הלידה:
notes.en: Her limbs become disjointed: because of the birth.

notes.he: אין דמה חוזר עליה עד עשרים וארבעה חדש ולפיכך מניקה אינה רואה דם נדה ולאו משום דדם נעשה חלב. והשתא כיון דלאו מחמת דם קאתי לאו חידוש הוא:
notes.en: And her soul does not return: her blood does not return to her until twenty-four months. That is why a nursing woman does not see menstrual blood, and not because the blood becomes milk. And now, since [milk] does not come from blood, it is no novelty.

notes.he: משום הכי דיה שעתה דאיבריה מתפרקין מחמת הלידה מחמת המניקות ואין נפשה כלומר אין דם ווסתה חוזר עליה עד כ"ד חדש שאינה בריאה כמו שהיתה עד כ"ד חדש הלכך דיה שעתה דאין לה דמים הרבה עד כ"ד חדש א"כ לטעמא דהא תנא ליכא למימר דחידוש הוא ומאי איצטריך אידך הגמל:
notes.en: But according to the one who says her time suffices for this reason: that her limbs become disjointed because of the birth, because of the nursing, and her soul does not, that is, the blood of her cycle does not return to her until twenty-four months, since she is not as healthy as she was until twenty-four months; therefore her time suffices, for she does not have much blood until twenty-four months. If so, by this tanna’s reasoning one cannot say it is a novelty, so why was the other “the camel” needed?

messages.text: It was necessary, because it might enter your mind to say it may be permitted; since generally speaking there is nothing that comes from a living animal that the Merciful One permits, and yet this milk of a kosher animal is similar to a limb severed from the living and is nevertheless permitted, the permissibility of milk is a novelty of the Torah. And consequently it might enter your mind to say that even the milk of a non-kosher animal should be permitted in line with that novelty. Therefore, the verse teaches us that it is forbidden.

notes.he: אכתי חדוש הוא הואיל דליכא מידי דאתי מחי דשרי והאי חלב כי אבר מן החי הוא ושרי היינו חידוש הלכך אפילו בבהמה טמאה נמי מישתרי להכי איצטריך קרא:
notes.en: It was necessary; it might enter your mind: it is still a novelty, since nothing that comes from a living being is permitted, and this milk is like a limb from the living and is permitted; that is the novelty. Therefore it would be permitted with a non-kosher animal too; that is why the verse was needed.

messages.text: § And from where do we derive that the milk of a kosher animal is in fact permitted?

If we say that it is derived from the fact that the Merciful One prohibits eating meat that was cooked in milk, indicating that milk by itself is permitted, one can reject this proof and say that milk alone is forbidden only for consumption but permitted with regard to deriving benefit from it. By contrast, meat that was cooked in milk is forbidden with regard to deriving benefit from it as well.

And according to Rabbi Shimon, who deems meat that was cooked in milk permitted with regard to deriving benefit from it, you find a reason for the Torah to mention the prohibition of meat and milk together, even if milk alone is forbidden as well, and that is in order to render one liable to receive lashes for cooking them together, which would not apply to cooking milk alone.

notes.he: לקמן בפירקין (בכורות דף י.) ר"ש אומר כו' משכחת לה דאיצטריך למיכתב בשר בחלב ואע"ג דחלב גרידא אסור נמי איצטריך למיכתב ביה ללקות על בישולו:
notes.en: And also according to Rabbi Shimon, who permits it for benefit: below in our chapter (the printed reference is Bekhorot 10a), Rabbi Shimon says, etc. You find that it was necessary to write meat in milk: even though milk alone is also forbidden, it was necessary to write it [so that one] receives lashes for cooking it.

notes.he: נמי דשרי לבשר בחלב בהנאה במס' חולין אפי' לטעמא דידיה לא מצית למימר דשרי דאע"ג דשרי לבשר בחלב בהנאה אי בשיל ליה בחלב לקי ואסור באכילה ואי בשיל לחלב לחודיה לא לקי אבל אסור באכילה ואכתי מנ"ל דשרי באכילה:
notes.en: And according to Rabbi Shimon too, who permits meat in milk for benefit, in tractate Ḥullin: even by his reasoning you cannot say it is permitted. For even though he permits meat in milk for benefit, if one cooked [meat] in milk he is flogged, while if one cooked the milk alone he is not flogged, though it is forbidden for eating. And still, from where do we know it is permitted for eating?

messages.text: Rather, one can prove that milk is permitted for consumption since the Merciful One revealed that with regard to disqualified consecrated animals that were redeemed: “You may slaughter and eat meat” (Deuteronomy 12:15). This verse is interpreted in the following manner: “You may slaughter,” but you may not use its wool from shearing. You may eat its “meat,” but you may not consume its milk. It can be inferred from here that milk of non-sacred kosher animals is permitted.

verse.he: רַק בְּכׇל־אַוַּת נַפְשְׁךָ תִּזְבַּח ׀ וְאָכַלְתָּ בָשָׂר כְּבִרְכַּת יְהֹוָה אֱלֹהֶיךָ אֲשֶׁר נָתַן־לְךָ בְּכׇל־שְׁעָרֶיךָ הַטָּמֵא וְהַטָּהוֹר יֹאכְלֶנּוּ כַּצְּבִי וְכָאַיָּל׃
verse.en: But whenever you desire, you may slaughter and eat meat in any of your settlements, according to the blessing that the ETERNAL your God has granted you. The impure and the pure alike may partake of it, as of the gazelle and the deer.

notes.he: רק בכל אות נפשך תזבח ואכלת בשר. בפסולי המוקדשין לאחר פדיונן הכתוב מדבר:
notes.en: You may slaughter: “However, with all the desire of your soul you may slaughter and eat meat.” The verse speaks of disqualified consecrated animals after their redemption.

notes.he: אלא מדגלי רחמנא גבי פסולי המוקדשין היכא דנאכלין במומן דכתיב תזבח דבספרי מוקים לה בפסולי המוקדשין תזבח ואכלת ולא גיזה דכתיב לא תגוז. ואכלת בשר ולא חלב דכתיב ולא תעבד דחולב בקדשין היינו עבודה מכלל דחלב בבהמה דחולין שרי באכילה:
notes.en: Rather, since the Merciful One revealed about disqualified consecrated animals, where they are eaten due to their blemish, as it is written “you may slaughter,” which the Sifrei sets as referring to disqualified consecrated animals: “you may slaughter and eat,” but not shearing, as it is written “you shall not shear”; “and eat meat,” but not milk, as it is written “nor work,” for milking consecrated animals is work. By inference, milk of a non-sacred animal is permitted for eating.

messages.text: But one could say the distinction between non-sacred milk and milk from sacrificial animals is not with regard to the permissibility of consumption. Rather, milk of non-sacred animals is forbidden for consumption but is permitted with regard to deriving benefit from it, but the milk of sacrificial animals is forbidden with regard to deriving benefit as well.

Rather, proof may be brought that milk is permitted from the fact that it is written: “And there will be goats’ milk enough for your food, for the food of your household, and maintenance for your maidens” (Proverbs 27:27). According to the verse, goats’ milk serves as food, and therefore must be kosher.

verse.he: וְדֵי ׀ חֲלֵב עִזִּים לְלַחְמְךָ לְלֶחֶם בֵּיתֶךָ וְחַיִּים לְנַעֲרוֹתֶיךָ׃
verse.en:
The goats’ milk will suffice for your food,
The food of your household,
And the maintenance of your maids.

messages.text: But perhaps the verse is referring to selling the milk as merchandise and using the money to buy food, and not to consuming the milk itself.

notes.he: ומוכרו להרויח בו כדי שיתפרנס:
notes.en: But perhaps for merchandise: and he sells it, to profit by it so that he can support himself.

messages.text: Rather, proof may be brought from the fact that it is written with regard to Jesse’s instructions to his son David upon sending him with provisions for his brothers, who were at war against the Philistines: “And these ten cheeses you shall bring to the captain of their thousand” (I Samuel 17:18), which indicates they ate dairy products.

verse.he: וְאֵת עֲשֶׂרֶת חֲרִצֵי הֶחָלָב הָאֵלֶּה תָּבִיא לְשַׂר־הָאָלֶף וְאֶת־אַחֶיךָ תִּפְקֹד לְשָׁלוֹם וְאֶת־עֲרֻבָּתָם תִּקָּח׃
verse.en: Take these ten cheeses to the captain of their thousand. Find out how your brothers are and bring some token from them.”

notes.he: גבינים וקא"ל ישי לדוד שיוליכם במלחמה לשר האלף:
notes.en: Ḥaritzei: cheeses. Jesse told David to bring them to the war, to the captain of the thousand.

messages.text: But perhaps this verse too means the captain can sell the cheese as merchandise.
Is that to say that it is the norm during war to engage in commerce? Clearly the cheese was meant for consumption, which proves it is permitted to eat dairy products.

notes.he: ודלמא לסחורה כדי שימכרם שר האלף לעובדי כוכבים וכי דרכה של מלחמה לסחורה הם רוצים להרוג את העובדי כוכבים וימכרו להם דבר מחיה אלא ש"מ לאכילת שר האלף עצמו הביאום:
notes.en: Ḥaritzei heḥalav: cheese. But perhaps for merchandise, so that the captain of the thousand could sell them to the gentiles? But is it the way of war to trade? They want to kill the gentiles; would they sell them provisions? Rather, learn from it that they brought them for the captain of the thousand himself to eat.

messages.text: And if you wish, say instead that proof may be brought from here: The Torah praises Eretz Yisrael as: “A land flowing with milk and honey” (Exodus 3:17), and if milk was not permitted, would the verse praise the land to us with an item that is not suitable for consumption?

verse.he: וָאֹמַר אַעֲלֶה אֶתְכֶם מֵעֳנִי מִצְרַיִם אֶל־אֶרֶץ הַכְּנַעֲנִי וְהַחִתִּי וְהָאֱמֹרִי וְהַפְּרִזִּי וְהַחִוִּי וְהַיְבוּסִי אֶל־אֶרֶץ זָבַת חָלָב וּדְבָשׁ׃
verse.en: and I have declared: I will take you out of the misery of Egypt to the land of the Canaanites, the Hittites, the Amorites, the Perizzites, the Hivites, and the Jebusites, to a land flowing with milk and honey.’

messages.text: And if you wish, say instead a proof from here: “Come, buy, and eat; and come, buy wine and milk without money and without price” (Isaiah 55:1).

verse.he: הוֹי כׇּל־צָמֵא לְכוּ לַמַּיִם וַאֲשֶׁר אֵין־לוֹ כָּסֶף לְכוּ שִׁבְרוּ וֶאֱכֹלוּ וּלְכוּ שִׁבְרוּ בְּלוֹא־כֶסֶף וּבְלוֹא מְחִיר יַיִן וְחָלָב׃
verse.en:
Ho, all who are thirsty,
Come for water,
Even if you have no money;
Come, buy food and eat:
Buy food without money,
Wine and milk without cost.

notes.he: וכתיב לעיל מיניה לכו שברו ואכלו:
notes.en: Wine and milk: and just before it is written, “come, buy, and eat.”

messages.text: § Returning to the dispute between Rabbi Shimon and the Rabbis, who interpret the repetition of the word “camel” as indicating the prohibitions against eating a camel born from a cow and consuming its milk, respectively: But if that is so, that the repetition indicates these halakhot, then with regard to the words: “Hare,” “hare,” “rock badger,” “rock badger,” “swine,” “swine” (see Leviticus 11:5–7; Deuteronomy 14:7–8), which are all mentioned twice as being forbidden, do these words come to teach these halakhot as well?

notes.he: בין לרבנן בין לר' שמעון דדרשי לעיל גמל גמל שפן שפן מאי דריש ביה:
notes.en: But if that is so: both according to the Rabbis and according to Rabbi Shimon, who expound “camel, camel” above, what do they expound from “rock badger, rock badger”?

notes.he: לרבנן דאמרי דגמל גמל לדרשא אתי לאסור חלב בהמה טמאה הכא נמי דשפן שפן וכו' דכתיבי תרי זמני להכי נמי הוא דאתי כו' הני למה לי אלא לא אתי אלא לכדתניא למה נשנו וכו' מפני השסועה דכל פרשה שנאמרה ונשנית לא נשנית אלא בשביל דבר שנתחדש בה:
notes.en: But if that is so: according to the Rabbis, who say “camel, camel” comes for an exposition, to prohibit the milk of a non-kosher animal, here too “rock badger, rock badger,” etc., which are written twice, do they come for this too? Why do I need them? Rather, they come only for what is taught: why were they repeated, etc., because of the shesua. For any passage that was stated and then repeated was repeated only for the sake of something new in it.

messages.text: They are necessary only for that which is taught in a baraita:

Why were all of the non-kosher animals and birds repeated in Deuteronomy (14:7–20), after having been mentioned already in Leviticus (11:10–20)? With regard to the animals, it is because of the shesua (see Deuteronomy 14:7), an animal with two backs and two spines, which is not mentioned in Leviticus, and with regard to the birds, it is because of the ra’a (see Deuteronomy 14:13).

notes.he: טמאים וטהורים:
notes.en: Why were the animals repeated: the non-kosher and the kosher ones.

notes.he: בריה שיש לה שני גבין ושני שדראות ולא נאמר בתורת כהנים:
notes.en: Because of the shesua: a creature that has two backs and two spines, and it is not mentioned in Torat Kohanim [Leviticus].

messages.text: If so, then the double reference of “camel,” “camel,” also comes for this purpose of teaching about the shesua, and not to teach a separate halakha about the camel.

notes.he: ולא לאסור חלב אתי:
notes.en: “Camel” too comes for this: and does not come to prohibit milk.

messages.text: Nevertheless, anywhere that it is possible to interpret the verse as teaching an additional halakha, we interpret it in that manner. Only where there is no possibility of such an interpretation is the concept of repeating the passage merely to introduce one additional detail invoked.

notes.he: לא אע"ג דאיכא למימר הכי דנשנו מפני השסועה מ"מ כל היכא דאיכא למידרש מידי דמשום הכי כתב דרשינן. ואמאי דרש לה מגמל גמל יותר דמשפן שפן וארנבת ארנבת משום דמההוא דנאמר תחלה דרשינן דהיינו גמל:
notes.en: No: even though one can say so, that they were repeated because of the shesua, nevertheless, wherever there is something to expound for which it was written, we expound it. And why does he expound from “camel, camel” rather than from “rock badger, rock badger” and “hare, hare”? Because we expound from the one stated first, which is the camel.

messages.text: § An additional source cites the opinion of Rabbi Shimon. The Sages taught in a baraita:

In the case of a ewe that gave birth to a goat of sorts and a goat that gave birth to a ewe of sorts, in each case the mother is exempt from its offspring being counted a firstborn. And if it has some of the characteristics of its mother, the mother is obligated, i.e., subject to accounting its offspring a firstborn.
The offspring does not have firstborn status unless its head and the majority of its body are similar to the appearance of its mother.

With regard to the permissibility of eating a non-kosher animal that was born to a kosher animal, does Rabbi Shimon require its head and most of its body to resemble its mother, or not, and possessing some of the characteristics of its mother suffices?
messages.lead: A dilemma was raised before the Sages:
messages.quote: unless its head and the majority of its body are similar to the appearance of its mother

notes.he: כגון פרה שילדה מין סוס דקאסר רבי שמעון כדקתני גמל גמל שני פעמים:
notes.en: With regard to eating: such as a cow that gave birth to a horse of sorts, which Rabbi Shimon forbids, as is taught: “camel, camel,” twice.

notes.he: דלא מישתרי באכילה במקצת סימנין עד שיהא ראשו ורובו דומה לאמו או לא:
notes.en: Does Rabbi Shimon require: that it is not permitted for eating with some of the characteristics until its head and most of it resemble its mother, or not?

notes.he: גבי טמא שנולד מן הטהור דאסר ר' שמעון באכילה כי אין בו מקצת סימנים כדאמרינן ר' שמעון אומר גמל ב' פעמים כו' אבל כי יש בו מקצת סימנים דומה לאמו שרי באכילה. מי בעי ר' שמעון עד שיהא ראשו ורובו דומה לאמו או בציר מהכי:
notes.en: A dilemma was raised before them, regarding eating: regarding a non-kosher [offspring] born from a kosher one, which Rabbi Shimon forbids for eating when it does not have some of the characteristics, as we said, “Rabbi Shimon says: camel, twice,” etc.; but when it has some of the characteristics resembling its mother, it is permitted for eating. Does Rabbi Shimon require that its head and most of it resemble its mother, or less than that?

messages.text: With regard to the halakha of firstborn status, it is written: “But the firstborn of an ox” (Numbers 18:17), which indicates that it does not have firstborn status unless it is an ox and its firstborn is an ox. If its head and most of its body do not resemble an ox, it does not have firstborn status according to Rabbi Shimon.

verse.he: אַךְ בְּכוֹר־שׁוֹר אוֹ־בְכוֹר כֶּשֶׂב אוֹ־בְכוֹר עֵז לֹא תִפְדֶּה קֹדֶשׁ הֵם אֶת־דָּמָם תִּזְרֹק עַל־הַמִּזְבֵּחַ וְאֶת־חֶלְבָּם תַּקְטִיר אִשֶּׁה לְרֵיחַ נִיחֹחַ לַיהֹוָה׃
verse.en: But the firstlings of cattle, sheep, or goats may not be redeemed; they are consecrated. You shall dash their blood against the altar, and turn their fat into smoke as an offering by fire for a pleasing odor to GOD.

messages.text: But with regard to consumption, where Rabbi Shimon holds a camel born to a kosher animal is forbidden, perhaps it is only an ordinary-looking camel that the Merciful One states is forbidden, but if…

notes.he: היינו כי ראשו ורובו דומה לאמו. אבל לאכילה גמל ממש הוא דאמר רחמנא אסור הא אישתני מגמל אפי' מקצת שפיר דמי באכילה. או דלמא לא שנא דלגבי אכילה בעי נמי ראשו ורובו:
notes.en: “And the firstborn of an ox”: that is, when its head and most of it resemble its mother. But with regard to eating, it is an actual camel that the Merciful One said is forbidden, so if it differs from a camel even partly, it is fine for eating. Or perhaps there is no difference, and with regard to eating too he requires its head and most of it.

messages.text: The sentence and the dilemma continue on 7a: if it differs from an ordinary camel, is it permitted to eat, or does Rabbi Shimon require its head and most of its body to resemble its mother for eating too?
